transcript.content: Hello, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. Well, honestly, I'm just at my wit's end, and I really didn't know where else to turn because what brings me in is... well, it's my job. I work down at the dry cleaners, and I've been doing laundry and dry cleaning work for a long time, you know, and usually I can keep my head above water, but lately... I just cannot seem to keep my work in order anymore. It is like a tornado hits my station every single day. 

I've got the yellow claim tickets, the credit card receipts, all these little scribbled workshop notes about alterations or special stain treatments that the tailors leave me, and then the actual customer jobs themselves—the bags of clothes, the hangers, the comforters—and it all just gets piled together in this massive, overwhelming mountain on the counter. I look at it, and I just freeze. I literally do not know what to handle first. The other day, I had a pile so high I couldn't even find a lady's silk blouse because the tag was buried under a stack of receipts from Tuesday, and I just stood there shuffling papers around while she stared at me. It's just a complete mess, and I'm so frustrated with myself because I feel like I should be able to just sort it out, but the piles just keep growing and growing until I can't even see the wood of the desk...
Has this kind of difficulty organizing and keeping track of things been a problem for you since childhood or your school years, or is this something that started more recently as an adult?

Oh, Lord, no, it is definitely not a new thing. If my mother were still alive, she'd probably just sigh and tell you I've been exactly like this since the day I learned to walk. I mean, going all the way back to grade school... I remember it so clearly, even though it was, what, forty-something years ago? My teachers—Mrs. Gable in third grade especially, I still remember her face—they used to pull my mother aside at every single parent-teacher conference. 

They would always say the exact same thing to her. They’d say, "She is such a bright girl, really very bright, but she is just so scattered." That was the word they always used, scattered. And it was true, I really was! I was constantly talking out of turn, just blurting things out in the middle of a lesson because a thought popped into my head and I just couldn't hold it in for the life of me. And the lost papers... oh my goodness, my desk back then looked exactly like my counter at the dry cleaners does right now. Just a complete disaster area of crumpled-up spelling tests and permission slips shoved all the way to the back. 

My mother was always getting notes sent home because I was losing my homework, or I just wouldn't finish it. The teachers were constantly having to tap my desk and give me reminders to just finish my work. Like, "Focus, look at the paper, finish the math problems before recess." So, yeah, it's always been this way. And it’s just so exhausting, honestly, to be 54 years old and still dealing with the exact same messy desk, just with dry cleaning tags instead of spelling tests, you know? It really makes you feel like you haven't grown up at all sometimes, because no matter how hard I try to set up a system, I just end up right back where I started when I was eight years old.

This longitudinal pattern rules out F41.1 (anxiety), F32.9 (depression), and F42.9 (OCD), which do not typically present with this childhood-onset, cross-situational pattern of inattention/impulsivity.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a lifelong (since grade school, confirmed by teacher reports and parental feedback) pattern of inattentive symptoms—losing important papers/items, difficulty organizing tasks, being easily distracted, and impulsive blurting out—that persists into adulthood with clear functional impairment in her occupational role at the dry cleaners. The chronicity, childhood onset, and cross-situational impairment (school then, work now) support a diagnosis of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, combined presentation given both inattentive and impulsive features described (blurting out, talking out of turn) rather than a purely inattentive-only picture.
